# PicoCalc NetThing

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

Author: Thomas Dzubin    License: MIT    Version: see `VERSION` in
[`netthing_const.h`](netthing_const.h)

Wireless networking for the ClockworkPi **PicoCalc** with a **Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W**
(RP2350 and the CYW43 Wi-Fi chip). It lists the access points in range with
their signal strength, connects to one (the password is kept on the SD card in a scrambled form),
and is a Wi-Fi and network test and troubleshooting tool for finding out why a connection is slow or down. It runs on
a **Pico 2 W** (RP2350) and, with some smaller limits, on the older **Pico W** (RP2040); there is no Windows or Linux
build, because the program needs the wireless chip.

## What it does

After a splash screen the program scans and lists the access points in range with their signal strength, channel and
security type, and shows the details of the one you choose. You can join a network (typing its password, or using the one
saved on the SD card), see the address the access point gave the PicoCalc, and keep a list of saved networks.

Once connected, the **status screen** shows the addresses, a live signal strength and a strip of the signal over the last few
minutes. From there `T` opens the **Wi-Fi tools menu**, `L` the **LAN tools menu** and `B` the **Bluetooth menu**.

The **Wi-Fi tools** are about the radio: a signal meter and a channel survey, for finding the best spot and the quietest
channel, and the health check ("is it working?" with traffic lights and a plain sentence), which is in the LAN tools menu too.

The **LAN tools** are for the network behind the radio: the health check, ping, ping the router, continuous ping with a graph and a log
file, trace route, a DNS checker, name lookup, a speed test, a web page check (the status code a server answers with, not the page),
setting the clock from an NTP time server, an update of the https certificates from inside the program, a scan of the local network
with a map of its devices, a port check, and, in a menu of their own because most people who run the program will not have the
server, the tools for the Windows test server (download and upload speed to it, a latency test, and a talk with it).

The **Bluetooth tools** (the Pico 2 W's chip does Bluetooth too): a scan of the devices around, finding one by its signal, reading
  what a device says about itself, a tracker alert and a 2.4 GHz crowding report.

Most tools draw a picture as well as the text (see "Pictures" below).

## What you need

- a ClockworkPi **PicoCalc** with a **Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W** (or a Pico W) in it. A plain Pico or Pico 2 has no wireless chip, so
  the program cannot work on it: it says `NO WIRELESS CHIP FOUND` and waits for `ESC`;
- an SD card in the PicoCalc, formatted FAT32 (the program keeps its files in a `/netthing/` folder on it);
- for https only: a list of trusted root certificates, `/netthing/CA.PEM`. The program has 32 roots built in and offers to write
  the file to the card the first time https needs it, so you need to do nothing (see "Setting up https");
- optional: a Windows PC for the test server, `netthing-server-Windows.exe`.

The quick start is: copy `netthing-RP2350.uf2` to the PicoCalc in BOOTSEL mode (see "Flashing"), press a key on the splash
screen, pick your network from the list and type its password. `~` (SHIFT + backtick) reboots into BOOTSEL from any screen,
and `ESC` or `Q` on the splash screen leaves for the PicoCalc UF2 Loader.

IPv6 works alongside IPv4. When your router advertises IPv6, the PicoCalc makes itself a global address and a
link-local one, and the status screen shows both (`NONE YET` until the router has answered). A name is looked up
IPv4 first and IPv6 is used only when the name has no IPv4 address. You can type an IPv6 address in ping, lookup,
the test server and NTP tools, and write it in square brackets in a web address
(`http://[2001:db8::1]:8080/`). https to a bare address cannot pass the certificate check, so use names there.
The Windows test server listens on IPv6 as well and prints all its addresses when it starts.

## The network tools

Each tool asks for what it needs and offers the last host you used again (they are kept as plain text in
`/netthing/SETTINGS.TXT` on the SD card). `ESC` stops one at any time.

## Bluetooth tools

The Pico 2 W's wireless chip does Bluetooth (Low Energy and Classic) as well as Wi-Fi, and the program uses it to look at the
Bluetooth devices around. Open them with `B` on the status screen or on the Wi-Fi scan list (no Wi-Fi connection is needed for the scan list).
The radio is switched on when the Bluetooth menu opens, which takes a second or two (the chip's Bluetooth firmware is loaded), and
off again when you leave it, so Wi-Fi has the chip to itself the rest of the time. What the program can see is what devices announce
about themselves; it cannot see the traffic between two other devices, and it cannot read anything that is encrypted.

- **Nearby devices (S):** a list of the Low Energy devices around, strongest signal first, with the name (or the maker and the end of
  the address, when it gives no name), signal bars and dBm, and what kind of device it seems to be (phone, computer, watch, audio,
  input, tracker, beacon, health, sensor), worked out from what it announces. A name in yellow has not been heard for 15 seconds.
  Below the list is a **Classic area** with four rows of the Classic devices (phones, computers, headsets, older speakers and car kits), strongest first; the heading shows `1-4 OF 17` when there are more, and the cursor scrolls through them. The Low Energy scan runs
  in windows of 5 seconds, and after four windows it stops for one Classic inquiry (about 10 to 15 seconds, with the names asked for
  afterwards), then carries on; the right end of the Classic heading shows `LE 1/4` to `LE 4/4`, `SEARCHING` or `PAUSED`. `P` pauses.
  The cursor runs down the Low Energy list and on into the Classic rows. `Enter` is the connect key (for tethering to a Classic phone;
  it says so for now, because tethering is not built yet) and `D` shows the details of any row.
  `Enter` shows the details: the address and whether it is a private one that changes (phones do this), the maker, the services it
  announces, the signal and how often it is heard. Phones often change their address every few minutes, so one phone may show up as
  several devices.
- **Find one (F):** choose a device and a wide signal meter follows it as its adverts arrive, with the best and the worst, a strip of
  the last readings, and WARMER or COLDER as you walk. Use it to find a lost tag or earbuds, or to see where a sensor drops out.
- **Read a device (I):** connects to a Low Energy device and reads its name, maker, model, firmware and battery level (a green,
  yellow or red bar) and the list of its services, then lets go. Many devices accept only one connection, or only their owner's phone;
  the screen then says it failed and suggests turning off the phone's Bluetooth.
- **Tracker alert (T):** looks for the tags that can be found with a phone (Apple's Find My network, Tile and Samsung SmartTag) and shows
  how long each has been in range. A tag that stays in range for many minutes while you move about (yellow after 5 minutes, red
  after 15) is probably with you and may not be yours. A Find My advert can also come from an Apple device that is away from its
  owner, and tags change their address now and then, so the time in range is the sign, not the address. It sees only tags that
  announce themselves in the usual way.
- **2.4 GHz crowding report (X):** Wi-Fi and Bluetooth use the same band, and this chip's antenna. It listens to both for ten seconds,
  draws the Wi-Fi networks on each channel, counts the Bluetooth devices (and how many are close), and says whether the band is quiet,
  busy or crowded, which is a common cause of a slow link or choppy audio.

## Pictures

Most tools draw a picture as well as the text; the colours are the same everywhere: green is good, yellow is fair, red is
poor, white is "no answer" or a frame. The ping scale is green up to 50 ms, yellow up to 150 ms, red above.

| Where | Picture |
|---|---|
| Status screen | a strip of the signal strength, one bar for each update (every 1.5 seconds), the last few minutes |
| Ping (P, R) | a bar for each of the four replies; a white full-height bar is a request with no answer |
| Continuous ping | the scrolling graph of the last 100 answers, with the signal above it |
| Signal meter (M) | one wide bar for the signal strength now, the best and worst seen, and the last 15 seconds below it |
| Speed test (B and the server download) | a bar for every half second of the download, so dips and stalls show, drawn as the test runs |
| DNS checker (D) | after the text, a chart of the four servers' average times with a line from the fastest to the slowest answer |
| Trace route (T) | after the text, one bar for each hop as long as its time; `x/3` marks a hop that lost requests |
| Channel survey (S) | bars (the strongest signal on each channel) or, with `V`, a hill for every network over the channels it covers, with the names of the strongest three |
| Port check | after the text, a grid of squares: green open, a white frame closed, yellow no answer; the arrow keys show each port |
| LAN scan | with `M`, a map with a square for every address of the range: green answers ping, yellow does not, white is the router, cyan is this PicoCalc, a dot is nothing; arrows show the address and MAC |
| Latency test (server menu) | a histogram of the 100 round trips in six bands of time |
| Health check | six lights, each with its reason |

- **Health check (H in the Wi-Fi tools menu and in the LAN tools menu):** answers "is it working?" for someone who does not know the tools. It runs from the radio
  outwards, each check with a light and a short reason: the Wi-Fi signal (bars), the router (three pings), DNS (the router's
  DNS server asked for example.com), the internet by ping (three pings to 1.1.1.1), the internet by connection (a TCP
  connection to 1.1.1.1 port 443, which works even where ping is blocked), and whether the PicoCalc has an IPv6 address (shown
  in cyan, since not having one is not a fault). Then one or two plain sentences, in this order of importance: weak signal; the
  router does not answer (a Wi-Fi or router problem); the router is fine but the internet is not reachable (modem or
  provider); names do not resolve (a DNS problem); it works but something is slow or losing packets; or everything looks good.
  `R` runs it again.
- **Ping (LAN tools menu P):** four echo requests one second apart, as Windows does, each with its time, then sent,
  received, lost, shortest, longest and average. With no host saved it offers the gateway.
- **Ping the router (LAN tools menu R):** the same four requests, sent at once to the gateway
  address the access point gave, with no questions asked. A router that answers in a few milliseconds and a
  failing ping to the internet means the problem is beyond the router; no answer from the router means the problem is
  the Wi-Fi link or the router itself.
- **Continuous ping (LAN tools menu C):** one request a second until `ESC`. The top shows the signal strength, the middle a graph of the
  last 100 answers (green up to 50 ms, yellow up to 150 ms, red above; a white full-height bar is a request with no
  answer; the scale of the tallest bar adjusts to the slowest answer shown), and below it the figures: sent, lost and
  percent lost, last, shortest, average and longest time, and jitter (the average change from one answer to the next). `L`
  starts or ends a log: `/netthing/PINGLOG.CSV` gets a line per request with the count, seconds since the start, the time
  in milliseconds (-1 for no answer), the signal in dBm and the clock time if it is set. `C` clears the figures. Walk
  around with the PicoCalc to find where the signal drops or answers get slow.
- **Trace route (LAN tools menu T):** sends requests with a hop limit that grows by one so that every router on the way
  answers in turn; three requests per hop with their times, and the router's address, until the target answers (shown
  in green), 30 hops, or six hops in a row with no answer at all. Many routers do not answer at all, which shows as
  `* * *`. Works with IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
- **Port check (LAN tools menu O):** asks for a host and a list of TCP ports (`80,443` or `20-25`, up to 64) and tries to
  connect to each: `OPEN` with the connect time, `CLOSED` (the host refused), or `NO ANSWER` after two seconds (a
  firewall that drops the request, or the host is off). Well-known ports are named. The list is remembered.
- **LAN scan (LAN tools menu S):** asks for the first and last address to scan (the hosts of your network, or the range you used
  last time on this network; at most 1024 addresses, and a network wider than a /24 is cut to the 254 addresses around
  your own). It sends an ARP request for every address in batches of eight and collects the devices that answer from the
  ARP table, which finds nearly everything on the network, even a device that does not answer ping. Then it pings each one
  found. The list shows each device's address, MAC address and ping time (`-` if it did not answer ping), sorted by
  address, with `R` marking the router and `T` this PicoCalc. A MAC address in cyan is a private one that the device made
  up for itself (many phones and computers do this per network), so it says nothing about the maker. `ESC` during the scan
  stops it and shows what was found so far. Only devices on your own network can be found this way.
- **Channel survey (Wi-Fi tools menu S):** scans and draws a bar for each 2.4 GHz channel 1 to 13, as tall as the strongest
  signal on it, with the number of networks under it (`+` is ten or more). The channel of the network you are
  connected to is yellow. It names the quietest of the three channels that do not overlap (1, 6, 11) by a crowding
  score that counts every network within four channels, the nearer and stronger the more.
- **DNS checker (LAN tools menu D):** asks for a name (the lookup name by default) and sends the same question straight to four DNS
  servers: your router's (the one the access point gave), Cloudflare (1.1.1.1), Google (8.8.8.8) and Quad9 (9.9.9.9). Each
  is asked three times for the IPv4 address and once for the IPv6 address. It shows the first address answered, the
  fastest, average and slowest time, and how many IPv6 addresses came back, or why there was no answer (timeout, name not
  found, server failure, refused). A plain verdict follows: no server answers; your router's DNS does not answer but the
  public ones do; your router's DNS is slow (more than 50 ms and three times the fastest public one); it says the name
  does not exist while the public ones find it; its answers share no address with the public ones (often harmless, since
  content networks answer differently from place to place); or DNS looks healthy. The questions go to each server
  directly, so this finds a bad router DNS even when the rest of the program seems to work.
- **Speed test (LAN tools menu E):** downloads a file for up to 10 seconds or 8 MB, whichever comes first, and throws the data
  away (nothing is written to the SD card, so the card cannot slow it). It shows a live figure while it runs and then the
  amount, the average in KB/s and Mbit/s, and the fastest half second. Type the address of a big file; the default is
  `http://speedtest.tele2.net/10MB.zip` and your last one is remembered. http is faster than https on this processor, so
  use http for a fair figure. The test measures the whole path to that server (Wi-Fi, your internet connection and the
  server), so use the Windows server tools to measure only the Wi-Fi link.
- **Name lookup (LAN tools menu N):** asks the DNS server (the one the access point gave) for a host's IPv4 address.
- **Windows test server tools (LAN tools menu V):** these need `netthing-server-Windows.exe` (the version that goes with this program, in this
  folder) running on a PC on the same network; type the PC's address it prints and its port (7000). Nothing else in the
  program needs it.
  - **Download speed:** the same speed test, against the server's `/stream` page, so only your Wi-Fi link and the PC are
    measured, not the internet.
  - **Upload speed:** sends data to the server for 10 seconds (or 16 MB) and shows the speed the server measured, from its
    first byte to its last.
  - **Latency test:** 100 small messages one at a time, each waiting for the server's echo (so it needs no ping): the
    shortest, average and longest time, the jitter, how many were lost and how many took more than 100 ms. A Wi-Fi link
    in power-saving mode or with interference shows spikes.
  - **Talk to a server:** connects to a host and port (7000 by default), sends one line and shows the
  reply. The `netthing-server-Windows.exe` test server in this folder answers it: run it on a PC on the
  same network, and type the address it prints. Windows Firewall will ask once whether to allow it; the
  PicoCalc needs a private-network allow. Nothing else in the program needs the test server.
- **Set the clock (LAN tools menu K):** asks an NTP server (pool.ntp.org by default) for the time and your offset from
  UTC (for example `-6` or `5:30`; there is no automatic daylight saving). The status screen then shows
  the running time. The clock is only in memory and starts again at the next power-up.

- **Web page check (LAN tools menu G):** type an address (`http://` or `https://`; the scheme may be left out). The program
  connects, asks for the page, reads only the status line and headers, and closes. It shows each redirect it
  followed (up to five), the final address, the status (`200 OK`, `404 Not Found`...) with a plain "the page exists" or
  "does not exist", the server's name, the content type and length, and how long the connection and the reply took.
  The page itself is not shown or kept.
- **https:** the connection is TLS 1.2, and the server's certificate is checked against the root certificates in
  `/netthing/CA.PEM` on the SD card (see "Setting up https" below). Checking needs the date, so the program sets the clock
  from the NTP server first if `W` has not been used. A site that offers only TLS 1.3 will fail. If the check fails (an unknown
  certificate authority, a wrong date, a certificate that has expired), the screen says so; the usual fixes are the certificate update
  (LAN tools menu U) and setting the clock (LAN tools menu K).

## Updating the certificates from the PicoCalc (LAN tools menu U)

`U` in the LAN tools menu refreshes `/netthing/CA.PEM` without a PC:

1. It downloads `https://curl.se/ca/cacert.pem.sha256` and `https://curl.se/ca/cacert.pem` (about 190 KB) into
   `/netthing/DOWNLOAD/`. These downloads are themselves checked with the `CA.PEM` that is there now, so the
   first `CA.PEM` must come from the `sdcard/` folder (see below); if there is none, the tool says so.
2. It computes the SHA-256 of the list and compares it with the downloaded checksum. If they differ, nothing is changed.
3. It keeps the roots named in `/netthing/CA-WANT.TXT` (one name per line, exactly as in the list; lines that start with
   `#` are ignored). If that file is missing, the tool writes it with the 32 built-in names, so you can edit it on a
   PC. The roots are written to a new `CA.PEM` (at most 48 KB); the old file is first copied to `/netthing/CA.BAK`, and put
   back if the new one cannot be made.
4. It reports how many roots were written and which wanted names were not in the list.

The next https connection uses the new file at once. If the PicoCalc's own copy has become so old that `curl.se` no longer
checks out, copy a fresh `CA.PEM` made on a PC (next section) onto the card.

## Setting up https (the CA.PEM file)

https needs a list of the certificate authorities you trust, as a text file named **`CA.PEM`** in the
**`/netthing/`** folder of the SD card. http pages need no file.

**The automatic way.** The program has the same 32 roots built in. When https needs `CA.PEM` and the card has none (or you
start the certificate update, LAN tools menu U), it says `THERE IS NO CERTIFICATE FILE ON THE CARD` and asks `WRITE THE BUILT-IN ONE TO THE
CARD? Y/N`. Press `Y` and the file is written to `/netthing/CA.PEM`, and the https check goes on. The update (LAN tools menu U) then
keeps it fresh. After you make a new `sdcard/netthing/CA.PEM` (below), run
`python tools/make_ca_header.py sdcard/netthing/CA.PEM ca_builtin.h` and rebuild to change the built-in list.

**A ready-made file.** This project's `sdcard/` folder holds `netthing/CA.PEM` with 32 widely
used roots (Let's Encrypt, DigiCert, GlobalSign, Google Trust Services, Amazon, Microsoft, Sectigo, GoDaddy,
USERTrust and a few more; the names are in `sdcard/CA-LIST.txt`). Copy the `netthing` folder from `sdcard/` onto
the root of the SD card, merging with the `netthing` folder that is already there. The card then has
`/netthing/CA.PEM` (about 37 KB).

**Making your own.** The roots come from the Mozilla list that the curl project publishes:

1. Download <https://curl.se/ca/cacert.pem> and its checksum <https://curl.se/ca/cacert.pem.sha256>, and check that
   they agree (`sha256sum cacert.pem` on Linux, `Get-FileHash cacert.pem` in PowerShell). The list is under the
   Mozilla Public License 2.0.
2. Choose the roots. The program reads at most **48 KB** of `CA.PEM` and keeps all of its certificates in memory during
   a connection, so use a short list, not all of the roughly 120. `tools/make_ca_pem.py` does it:

   ```bash
   python tools/make_ca_pem.py cacert.pem CA.PEM            # the same 32 roots as the ready-made file
   python tools/make_ca_pem.py cacert.pem --list            # every root name in the list
   python tools/make_ca_pem.py cacert.pem CA.PEM mine.txt   # the roots named in mine.txt, one per line
   ```

3. Copy `CA.PEM` to the SD card as `/netthing/CA.PEM`.

A site whose certificate chains to a root that is not in your file fails the check. To add the root, find its
name in the list (`--list`), put it in your names file, and make the file again. Root lists change, so make a
new `CA.PEM` once a year or so. A copy of `CA.PEM` that someone else gives you is only as trustworthy as that
person: it decides which sites the PicoCalc believes.

## Files on the SD card

Everything is in the `/netthing/` folder; the program makes it when it first writes. Only `CA.PEM` has to be put there by
hand, and only for https.

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `WIFI.DAT` | the saved networks, scrambled |
| `SETTINGS.TXT` | the hosts, ports, web address, time offset and scan range last used (plain text) |
| `CA.PEM`, `CA.BAK`, `CA-WANT.TXT` | the trusted root certificates for https, the copy kept by the update, the names to keep |
| `PINGLOG.CSV` | the log of a continuous ping, if you started one |
| `DOWNLOAD/` | the certificate update's downloads |

## Modes and the title screen

After the title screen the program is always in one of three modes: the **Wi-Fi scan**, the **Bluetooth scan** or the **LAN tools**
menu. `B` and `L` (on the scan screens) and `W` and `B` (in the LAN tools menu) move between them. `ESC` in a mode goes back to the
title screen, and any key there carries on in the mode that was left (the Wi-Fi scan the first time, and also if the LAN tools have
no connection any more). Going to the title screen does not drop the connection, so a stray `ESC` costs nothing. `ESC` or `Q` on
the title screen leaves the program. A scan that was paused starts again when you come back to it from another screen, except that
the Wi-Fi scan stays paused while a connection is up.

## Reaching the LAN: Wi-Fi, USB and Bluetooth (work in progress)

The program is first of all a wireless scanning tool (the Wi-Fi scan and the Bluetooth scan work without any connection). To use the LAN
tools it must be connected to a network, by **one** of these ways at a time; connecting a second way asks first to give up the one that is up.
The top line of every screen says how it is connected.

- **Wi-Fi:** `Enter` on a network in the Wi-Fi scan. Done and working.
- **IP over USB (new, written but not yet tried on real hardware):** press `U` on the title screen. The PicoCalc's USB port then shows up on a
  PC as a network adapter (CDC NCM; Windows 10 and 11 load their own driver for it, and Linux and macOS do too). Plug the PicoCalc into the
  PC with a USB data cable, and share the PC's internet connection with the new adapter; on Windows: Settings, Network & Internet, Advanced
  network settings, More network adapter options, right-click the adapter that has the internet (Wi-Fi or Ethernet), Properties, Sharing,
  tick *Allow other network users to connect*, and choose the new adapter (its name is *Ethernet* and a number; unplug and plug the PicoCalc
  to see which one appears). Windows then gives the adapter 192.168.137.1 and its DHCP server gives the PicoCalc an address; the top line
  of the screen shows `USB 192.168.137.x` and the LAN tools open. `ESC` while it waits cancels. The PC's firewall may block pings to it.
  USB networking uses the wireless chip's driver for the network stack, so it needs a Pico W or Pico 2 W like everything else.
- **Bluetooth tethering (in progress, not working yet):** the Bluetooth scan already lists the Classic phones around (the Classic area); `Enter`
  on one is meant to connect to its shared connection (the PAN profile) and for now only says so. The code in `tether.c` is the start of it.

## Saved networks

After a password you typed has worked, the program asks `SAVE THIS NETWORK? Y/N`. The names and
passwords of saved networks (up to 16) go in `/netthing/WIFI.DAT` on the SD card. The file is
**scrambled, not encrypted**: it reads as noise and differs at every save, so a card put in
other hardware shows no plain text password, but the key is in the program, so anyone who has
the program can undo it. A saved password that the access point later refuses is not removed
automatically: forget it with `S` and `D`.

The file also keeps the BSSID (the address) of the access points you joined, up to four per
network. The program reads the file when it starts the scan and keeps it in memory, and every
save updates both. In the scan list the name of an access point is shown in **green** when a
saved network has both its name and its BSSID, and in **yellow** when only one of them is saved
(the same name on an access point not joined before, or a saved BSSID under another name, or a
saved network that has no BSSID yet). Joining a saved network adds the BSSID of the access
point you reached, so a yellow name turns green after the first connection. A file from an
earlier version is still read; the next save writes the new kind.

## Building

You need the Pico SDK (2.3.0 here) **with its `cyw43-driver`, `lwip`, `mbedtls` and `btstack` folders
filled in** (a plain zip download of the SDK has them empty), and a Pico 2 W:

```bash
cmake -B build-rp2350 -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w
ninja -C build-rp2350
```

The result is **`netthing-RP2350.uf2`**, also copied to this folder. Run the build from
PowerShell on Windows, not Git Bash (see the Pico notes in the author's lessons file).

## The Pico W (RP2040) build

The same program builds for the older Pico W, as `netthing-RP2040.uf2`. That chip has 264 KB of RAM against the Pico 2 W's 520 KB,
so this build has smaller limits: the https certificate list holds about 15 roots (the first ones of `CA.PEM`; the rest are
ignored), the Bluetooth device list holds 32 devices, and the network buffers are smaller, so very large web pages may be slower.
The tools for the Windows test server are left out of this build (they took about 6.5 KB of program space and 5.8 KB of RAM), so the
LAN tools menu has no `V`. Everything else is the same. It has been compiled but **not run on real hardware**: its author has only a Pico 2 W.

```bash
cmake -B build-rp2040 -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico_w
ninja -C build-rp2040
```

## Flashing

Hold BOOTSEL while powering the PicoCalc on, or press `~` in the program. A
drive named `RP2350` (`RPI-RP2` on a Pico W) appears; copy the `.uf2` file onto it. The program starts at once.

## The Windows test server

`tools/netserver.c` is a small test server for Windows (Winsock). Build it with MinGW gcc:

```bash
gcc -O2 -Wall -o netthing-server-Windows.exe tools/netserver.c -lws2_32
```

Run it on a PC on the same network; it prints the addresses to type on the PicoCalc and listens on port 7000 (or the port
given on the command line) for IPv4 and IPv6. Windows Firewall asks once whether to allow it; allow it on private networks.
It answers a line of text, serves a few test web pages (`/`, `/text`, `/redirect`, `/missing`, `/chunked`, `/big`, `/stream`), takes
an upload at `/upload` and echoes a latency test. Only the tools in the server menu need it.

## PC tests

The portable parts have tests that build with any C compiler; the compile line is in the header of each file in `tests/`, for
example:

```bash
gcc -O1 -Wall -Wextra -I. tests/lan_test.c lanscan.c -o lan_test && ./lan_test
```

Each prints PASS or FAIL for every check and exits with the number of failures.

### Third-party

`picocalc-text-starter-main/` is a vendored copy of
[**picocalc-text-starter**](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter)
by Blair Leduc (the LCD, audio and south-bridge keyboard drivers). It is **not**
relicensed by this project: it keeps its own MIT license at
[`picocalc-text-starter-main/LICENSE`](picocalc-text-starter-main/LICENSE),
Copyright © 2025 Blair Leduc. The Raspberry Pi Pico SDK it builds against is
licensed separately by Raspberry Pi Ltd. (BSD-3-Clause); the Wi-Fi driver (cyw43-driver),
the TCP/IP stack (lwIP) and mbedTLS that come with it have their own licences. The Bluetooth stack is **BTstack** by BlueKitchen GmbH,
which comes with the SDK in `lib/btstack` and is not part of this project. Its licence allows use with Raspberry Pi's wireless
products (Pico W, Pico 2 W) under the terms in the SDK's `src/rp2_common/pico_btstack/LICENSE.RP` and `lib/btstack/LICENSE` (read them,
they limit use to those products and to non-commercial use); this project is for the Pico 2 W and is free.
The USB network adapter uses **TinyUSB** (by Ha Thach, MIT licence), which also comes with the SDK, and `usbnet_desc.c` is adapted from its
`net_lwip_webserver` example (its licence text is at the top of that file).

The vendored copy is unchanged except for these fixes, all in `drivers/`:

1. `fat32.c`: `get_next_free_cluster()` advances its search hint past the cluster it just
   handed out; without that, every later allocation re-scans the clusters already given out.
2. `fat32.c`: `fat32_dir_read()` skips deleted entries before it looks at long-name parts, and
   copes with the last part of a long name (a deleted long-name part used to be read as a live
   one and wrote past the end of a stack buffer); `link_entry()` compares the 0xE5 deleted
   marker as an unsigned byte.
3. `sdcard.c`: the wait for a busy card is timed by the clock (0.5 s), every command except CMD0
   waits for the card first (and is not sent if the card stays busy), and a write returns an
   error if the card is still busy after it.
4. `fat32.c`: `fat32_write()` no longer allocates a cluster twice when a write starts on a
   cluster boundary (a lost cluster each time), and returns at once for a write of zero bytes.
5. `lcd.c`: `lcd_putstr()` cuts a string off at the right edge of the display instead of
   overrunning its one-row line buffer.

Fixes 2 and 3 were sent to the author as pull requests; 4 is prepared but not sent. Everything
else is exactly as downloaded.
